titulo_es: So, such, too and enough (degree and result)
descripcion_es: Intensifying with so and such, expressing excess with too and sufficiency with enough; position and structures with that and the infinitive.
resumen: So and such intensify (Spanish “tan”, “tal”) and can introduce a result with that. Too indicates excess (more than necessary) and enough, sufficiency (as much as necessary). Each one has a fixed position.

filas: The film was so boring that I fell asleep.
It was such a boring film that I fell asleep.
too + adjective (+ for someone) (+ to infinitive)
This coffee is too hot to drink.
He isn't old enough to vote.

items: Such a/an with a singular countable noun: such a nice day. No article with plurals and uncountable nouns: such nice people, such bad weather.
So with much, many, few, little: so many people, so much money.
Too has a negative meaning (excess): It's too expensive = I can't buy it. For a positive “very”, use very or so.
Enough goes AFTER the adjective but BEFORE the noun: warm enough / enough time.

explicacion.texto: Do not confuse too (more than necessary) with too much / too many (too + noun): too much sugar, too many cars. Before an adjective on its own, never too much: too tired, not too much tired.

ejemplos.frase: She was so tired that she went to bed at eight.
ejemplos.traduccion: Estaba tan cansada que se acostó a las ocho.

ejemplos.frase: They're such good friends that they went on holiday together.
ejemplos.traduccion: Son tan buenos amigos que se fueron juntos de vacaciones.

ejemplos.frase: The box is too heavy for me to carry.
ejemplos.traduccion: La caja pesa demasiado para que yo la lleve.

ejemplos.frase: Is the room big enough for six people?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Es la habitación lo bastante grande para seis personas?

ejemplos.frase: There were so many tourists that we couldn't see the painting.
ejemplos.traduccion: Había tantos turistas que no pudimos ver el cuadro.

ejemplos.frase: I didn't have enough time to finish the exam.
ejemplos.traduccion: No tuve tiempo suficiente para terminar el examen.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: It was a so beautiful day.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: It was such a beautiful day.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Before a noun, use such a, not a so.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He isn't enough tall to play basketball.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He isn't tall enough to play basketball.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I'm too much tired to go out.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I'm too tired to go out.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Before an adjective, use only too, without much.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: This town is too nice, I love it.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: This town is so nice, I love it.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Too implies negative excess; for praise, use so or very.

ejercicios.frase: It was ___ cold day that we stayed inside.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule from Rules and key points: such a/an goes before a singular countable noun, with or without an adjective. The clue is that after the gap comes “cold day”, an adjective plus a singular countable noun. That is why the intensifier is such a: “such a cold day that…”. So would only go with the adjective on its own: “The day was so cold that…”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hacía un día tan frío que nos quedamos dentro.

por_opcion.so: Incorrect: so goes with adjectives or adverbs on their own; before a noun (“cold day”), use such a.
por_opcion.such a: Correct: such a + adjective + singular countable noun (day).
por_opcion.too: Incorrect: too indicates excess and does not introduce a result with that; also, “too cold day” is not grammatical.

ejercicios.frase: The music was ___ loud that I couldn't hear you.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the first row of the table: so + adjective or adverb. The clue is that after the gap there is only the adjective loud, with no noun, followed by that, which introduces the result. That is why so is used: “so loud that I couldn't hear you”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Adjective on its own (loud) + that: so.
ejercicios.traduccion: La música estaba tan alta que no te oía.

por_opcion.so: Correct: so + adjective on its own (loud) + that for the result.
por_opcion.such: Incorrect: such needs a noun after it; here there is only an adjective.
por_opcion.enough: Incorrect: enough would go after the adjective (loud enough) and expresses sufficiency, not intensity with a result.

ejercicios.frase: She's ___ young to drive. She's only fifteen.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row for too: too + adjective (+ to infinitive) expresses an excess that prevents something. The clue is the second sentence: at fifteen he cannot drive, so his age is an obstacle. Too young to drive means that his age prevents him from driving; notice that too has the negative meaning pointed out in the card.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Excess that prevents something: too + adjective + to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es demasiado joven para conducir. Solo tiene quince años.

por_opcion.enough: Incorrect: enough would go after (young enough) and would say the opposite, that he is old enough.
por_opcion.too: Correct: excess that prevents driving, too + adjective + to.
por_opcion.such: Incorrect: such needs a noun and does not express excess.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the position rule from Rules and key points: enough goes before the noun but after the adjective. Here it goes with a noun, plates, so it goes before it: enough plates. The clue is that there is no adjective, only the noun. The order “plates enough” is archaic and is not used today.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay suficientes platos para todos.

por_opcion.plates enough: Incorrect: enough only goes after adjectives and adverbs; with nouns it goes before.
por_opcion.too plates: Incorrect: too does not go before nouns; for excess with plurals, say too many plates.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule from Rules and key points: such a/an only with singular countable nouns; with plurals and uncountable nouns, such without an article. The clue is neighbours, in the plural, preceded by the adjective nice. That is why you say “such nice neighbours”, without a.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Plural noun: such without an article.

por_opcion.such a: Incorrect: the article a cannot go with a plural noun (neighbours).
por_opcion.such: Correct: such without an article + adjective + plural noun.
por_opcion.so: Incorrect: so does not go before adjective + noun; it is used with the adjective on its own (they are so nice).

ejercicios.frase: I've never seen ___ much snow in Madrid.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule from Rules and key points: so with much, many, few and little. The clue is much right after the gap. Although a noun follows (snow), the intensifier goes with much, so so is used: “so much snow”, which is equivalent to Spanish “tanta nieve”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Nunca he visto tanta nieve en Madrid.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Such is not combined with much; the rule in the card is so much / so many.
Too much would mean more snow than necessary, with an idea of negative excess, and it does not fit with never seen.
Very much is not used before a noun in an affirmative sentence with this meaning; Spanish “tanta” is so much.

ejercicios.frase: It was ___ bad weather that the flight was cancelled.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of such without an article with uncountable nouns. The clue is weather, which is uncountable in English and therefore does not take a. As there is adjective + noun (bad weather), such is required, not so. The result is “such bad weather that the flight was cancelled”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Weather is uncountable: such without an article.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hacía tan mal tiempo que se canceló el vuelo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Weather is uncountable and does not take the article a; you say such bad weather.
So does not go before adjective + noun; with weather after it, use such.

ejercicios.frase: The water isn't warm ___ to swim.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the position rule: enough goes after the adjective. The clue is that the gap is between the adjective warm and to swim. The negative sentence with enough expresses that the necessary minimum is not reached. Too would not fit after the adjective, because it always goes before it.
ejercicios.traduccion: El agua no está lo bastante templada para bañarse.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Too goes before the adjective (too cold), never after it; here the position after warm requires enough.
A common spelling mistake: it is written enough.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with too much or too many.
ejercicios.frase: You put ___ salt in the soup.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the final note in the card: before a noun, “more than necessary” is too much or too many. The clue is salt, an uncountable noun, which requires much. Too on its own, without much, would go with an adjective (too salty).
ejercicios.traduccion: Has echado demasiada sal a la sopa.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Many is for plural countable nouns; salt is uncountable, so much is used.
Too on its own goes before an adjective; before a noun you need too much.
It expresses intensity (“such a lot of salt”) but not excess; the instruction asks for too much or too many.

ejercicios.frase: This jacket is enough big for me.
respuestas: This jacket is big enough for me.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the position rule from Rules and key points: enough goes after the adjective. The mistake in the sentence is copying the Spanish word order of “suficientemente grande”. The correct form is “big enough for me”, which expresses that the size meets what is needed. Remember that with nouns the order is reversed (enough room), but with adjectives enough always goes after.
ejercicios.traduccion: Esta chaqueta es lo bastante grande para mí.

errores_previstos.respuesta: This jacket is enough big for me.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: enough goes after the adjective.

errores_previstos.respuesta: This jacket is big enought for me.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The position is correct, but enough is misspelt.

errores_previstos.respuesta: This jacket is enough bigger for me.
errores_previstos.explicacion: No comparative is needed, and enough is still in the wrong position: big enough.

respuestas: He is such a good cook.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of such a + adjective + singular countable noun, and the typical mistake “a so” mentioned in the card. The clue is cook, a singular countable noun, preceded by the adjective good. The correct order is such + a + good + cook. Both the contracted and the full form of the verb are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Before a noun: such a + adjective + noun.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: before a noun, do not use a so, but such a.
So cannot go before the article; the structure is such a good cook.
Cook is singular countable and needs the article: such a good cook.

ejercicios.frase: The book was so interesting that I read it in one day.
respuestas: It was such an interesting book that I read it in one day.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the change from so + adjective to such + a/an + adjective + noun. You have to turn the adjective interesting into a modifier of a noun (book) and use it was as the subject. As interesting begins with a vowel sound, the article is an: “such an interesting book”. The result with that stays the same.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: So + adjective becomes such an + adjective + noun (an before a vowel).
ejercicios.traduccion: Era un libro tan interesante que lo leí en un día.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It was such a interesting book that I read it in one day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Before a vowel sound the article is an: such an interesting book.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It was a such interesting book that I read it in one day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The article goes after such: such an, not a such.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The book was such interesting that I read it in one day.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Such needs a noun after it; with the adjective on its own, you would keep so.

ejercicios.frase: The tea is very hot. I can't drink it.
respuestas: The tea is too hot to drink.
The tea is too hot for me to drink.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the structure from the table too + adjective (+ for someone) (+ to infinitive). The two sentences are joined by expressing that the excessive heat prevents drinking. The object it is not repeated at the end, because the subject, the tea, is already what is drunk. Adding for me, which the table presents as optional, is accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Too + adjective + to infinitive; it is not repeated.
ejercicios.traduccion: El té está demasiado caliente para bebérselo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The tea is too hot to drink it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object is not repeated: the subject (the tea) is already what cannot be drunk.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The tea is too much hot to drink.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Before an adjective, use only too, without much.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The tea is too hot for drink.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Purpose is expressed with to + infinitive, not with for + infinitive.

respuestas: she isn't old enough to vote
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the structure from the table adjective + enough + to infinitive. The order is subject + negative verb + adjective + enough + to vote. The key is to place enough after old, the opposite of Spanish “suficientemente mayor”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she isn't enough old to vote
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies Spanish word order: enough goes after the adjective, old enough.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she isn't old to enough vote
errores_previstos.explicacion: Enough goes immediately after the adjective and before to vote.

descripcion_larga_es: So and such intensify (Spanish “tan”, “tal”) and can introduce a result with that; too expresses excess (more than necessary) and enough, sufficiency (as much as necessary). They are small but very frequent words, and each one has a fixed position in the sentence. They are difficult for Spanish speakers because “tan” is translated in two ways depending on whether a noun follows, and because enough goes after the adjective.

contexto.que_es: They are four intensifiers with fixed structures. So goes with adjectives and adverbs (so boring) and with much, many, few, little; such goes with nouns, with or without an adjective (such a boring film, such bad weather). Too indicates excess (too hot) and enough, sufficiency (old enough, enough chairs).
contexto.por_que_importa: They are used constantly to express results (so… that), complaints, praise and limits (too young to drive). Confusing too with very or so changes the message: “this town is too nice” sounds like a reproach. Position mistakes (a so beautiful day, enough tall) are very noticeable and typical of B1-level exams.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: So and such appear when intensifying or expressing a result with that; too, when something prevents doing something else (too + adjective + to); enough, when a minimum is or is not reached. The signal for choosing between so and such is whether a noun follows. Spanish speakers tend to say “a so” for “tan”, “too much tired” for “demasiado cansado” and “enough tall” following the order of “suficientemente alto”.
